The export-led development model that has propelled China’s growth to this point has just about run out of steam. China’s future growth, and its ability to vault over the much dreaded middle income trap, will be dependent on its ability to navigate the tricky transition away from low-cost exports (enabled by a favourable exchange rate) and towards greater domestic demand-driven growth. But as this fraught transition unfolds, the argument goes, there are limits to how much economic slowing Chinese officials will tolerate. With weakening exports compounded by anaemic domestic demand and lacklustre factory output — to say nothing of a massive debt overhang from the 2008–09 stimulus — even the comparatively modest growth rate target of 7 per cent is in jeopardy. Chinese policy makers are under increasing pressure to take measures to spark growth. texts.full_text: invention of this application relates to a high toughness steel and to a method for manufacturing the same. More particularly, the invention of this application relates to a high toughness steel having an excellent toughness useful for a steel material used as steel for structural purposes such as steel bars, section steel, thin plates and thick plates and also relates to a method for manufacturing the same. In a steel material which has been utilized as the steel for structural purposes, there is a problem that a prior-austenite grain boundary which is the weakest part or the inherent defects such as inclusions, segregation, or microvoids at the grain boundary may cause a reduction in toughness, especially under low-temperature or high-stress conditions. This is because the prior-austenite grain boundary, during phase transformation (e.g., from austenite to ferrite or bainite), becomes a preferential site for crack initiation and propagation, leading to brittle fracture. To address this issue, the invention proposes a high toughness steel with a controlled chemical composition and microstructure. The steel comprises, by mass, the following components: - Carbon (C): 0.05–0.20%, to ensure sufficient strength without compromising toughness. - Silicon (Si): 0.10–0.50%, as a deoxidizer and to refine grain size. - Manganese (Mn): 1.0–2.5%, to stabilize austenite and improve hardenability. - Aluminum (Al): 0.01–0.05%, for deoxidation and grain refinement. - Niobium (Nb): 0.01–0.05%, to refine grains and inhibit recrystallization during hot rolling. - Titanium (Ti): 0.005–0.02%, to form carbides/nitrides and further refine grains. - Optional

Left Pneumonectomy: The entire left lung is removed in this patient with lung cancer. Visible anatomy includes the pulmonary arteries and veins, bronchi, and the aorta. The latissimus dorsi, serratus anterior muscles are also visible as they form part of the lateral thoracic wall during dissection. During left pneumonectomy surgery: - Pulmonary Arteries: These large arteries carry deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to each lung for oxygenation. The main pulmonary artery divides into two branches, and in this case, one is dissected free as part of the procedure. - Pulmonary Veins: Typically there are four veins that return freshly oxygenated blood back to the left atrium of the heart from both lungs; they must be carefully identified during a pneumonectomy. On theleft side,two main branches—superior and inferior—are ligated, cut,and removed along withthe lung. - Bronchi: the bronchial tree is divided into primary (lobar) or secondary branch points that serve individual portions of each lobe; these structures are also carefully dissected during a pneumonectomy. In the left side,surgeries involve sealing off and dividing either one main stemor multiple segmentalbronchiolesdepending onthecase. - Aorta: The thoracic part is often seen prominently in open-chest procedures, serving as an anatomical landmark but rarely requiring direct surgical manipulation during lung resections. It’s important to maintain visibility of this structure throughout the surgery for safe dissection and orientation withinthe chest cavity. That means there are very few constraints on your actions or choices: they're entirely independent of what other people have done (and therefore don't affect them either). It seems to me that this makes for a completely different kind MMO. And the same goes even more so if we think about it in terms of "casual gamers". The idea is very simple, but also quite profound: Casually casual games are not just easy-to-learn. They're actually easier than learning any other game -- and therefore they have an advantage over all their competitors! So what does this mean for Legends? Well first off there's the obvious point: if it works out then we've got a whole new way to look at MMORPGs! (And that applies just as much, maybe more so too in fact , when you're talking about casual MMO games.) But beyond all of those implications -- which are already enough for me personally :-) there's something else. If Legends does succeed it'll be an example not only how this kind-of game works but also what kinds can work . And that could open up a whole new world (of gaming) to people who've never thought about these things before. So maybe the biggest question is whether or no we should all start thinking seriously now? Or at least give Legends our full support -- because if it succeeds then there'll be lots more like this.
